expected_behavior: Confirms Wear OS severs background TCP sockets roughly 5 seconds after wm_stop_activity (procState=LAST) even when on the charger with stay_on_while_plugged_in keeping the watch face awake.

Identifies adb shell dumpsys netpolicy (<uid>-background-default with blocked=APP_BACKGROUND|DATA_SAVER) and D/InetDiagMessage ('Destroyed live tcp sockets for uids={...}', ECONNABORTED errno 103), distinguishing the ~5s network cutoff from the ~60s am_freeze.
Recommends high-priority FCM push delivery rather than keeping a persistent Foreground Service running solely for an idle chat socket.
cases.prompt:
A developer is testing a standalone Wear OS chat app (com.example.watchchat) on a Pixel Watch running Wear OS 5 over Wi-Fi. When opened, the app connects a persistent TLS TCP socket to receive live chat messages. Before testing, the watch is placed on its magnetic charger and `adb shell settings put global stay_on_while_plugged_in 7` is enabled so the display stays awake on the watch face. While the chat activity is on screen, messages arrive immediately. The developer presses Home to view the watch face (still charging, screen still on), and incoming messages stop arriving within 10 seconds. A colleague argues Wear OS would not cut off the socket while charging with the screen awake, blaming an app lifecycle bug instead.

Does Wear OS itself cut off the backgrounded app's live TCP socket in this charging and screen-on state (and roughly how many seconds after leaving the activity), which `adb shell dumpsys` service and exact logcat tag directly prove the socket destruction, and what architecture should replace holding a background TCP socket open?

expected_behavior: Explains that polling a frozen app via adb shell run-as transiently unfreezes (thaws) the app process for roughly 5 seconds before re-freezing, creating an observer effect that invalidates background wake-up measurements.
Names the exact events-buffer logcat tag am_unfreeze (paired with subsequent am_freeze), rather than guessing ActivityManager or hallucinating that the eBPF freezer kills the process.
cases.prompt:
A tester backgrounds a debuggable app (`com.example.chat`) on a Pixel Watch running Wear OS 5, then runs this host script for 30 minutes to check whether anything wakes the backgrounded app process while monitoring `sync.db`'s mtime:

```bash
adb logcat -c
adb logcat -b all > watch_all.log &
LOG_PID=$!

for i in $(seq 1 30); do
  adb shell run-as com.example.chat stat -c '%Y' files/sync.db
  sleep 60
done

kill "$LOG_PID"
```

What specific OS process-state side effect does that `adb shell run-as` loop trigger on `com.example.chat` every 60 seconds, why does it invalidate the wake-up test, and what exact logcat tag in `watch_all.log` records it?

expected_behavior: Names gtalk_connection and gtalk_heartbeat_reset in adb logcat -b events, plus adb shell dumpsys activity service com.google.android.gms/.gcm.GcmService.
Clarifies that GcmService's hourly HiPri counter aggregates high-priority pushes device-wide across all packages on the watch (not per-UID), so per-app wakeups must be corroborated via am_unfreeze.
Uses ringing/locating the watch via Google Find Hub / Find My Device as a zero-install, credential-free high-priority FCM positive control.
cases.prompt:
A QA engineer is debugging push delivery for a standalone Wear OS app on an unrooted retail Pixel Watch connected directly to Wi-Fi, with its paired phone in Airplane Mode so nothing bridges over Bluetooth. Over a 10-minute wait, expected Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) pushes never wake the watch app. The engineer only has `adb` access to the watch, has no backend server or Firebase credentials, and cannot install extra test apps.

1. Which `events`-buffer logcat tags confirm Google Play Services' live push socket and heartbeats, and what does the hourly high-priority delivery counter in Play Services' push `dumpsys` output measure (per-package vs. device-wide across all watch apps)?
2. How can the engineer trigger an immediate, real end-to-end high-priority FCM push to the standalone watch as a positive control?

expected_behavior: Warns against static <meta-data android:name="com.google.android.wearable.notificationBridgeMode" android:value="NO_BRIDGING"/> in AndroidManifest.xml because it silences bridged phone alerts immediately on install before watch login.

Uses BridgingManager.fromContext(context).setConfig(BridgingConfig.Builder(context, false).build()) only after watch login + verified push readiness, and re-enables bridging with BridgingConfig.Builder(context, true).build() on logout.
Pairs disabled bridging with matching NotificationCompat.WearableExtender().setDismissalId(...) on both phone and watch notifications to preserve cross-device dismissal synchronization.
cases.prompt:
We ship an Android messaging app (`com.example.messenger`) alongside a standalone Wear OS watch app with the same package name. The watch APK is often auto-installed onto paired watches during watch setup before the user ever opens it, and requires QR / phone sign-in on the watch before it can receive its own FCM push messages and post notifications locally.

How should Wear OS notification bridging and cross-device notification dismissals be configured across pre-login, signed-in, and signed-out states so users never miss notifications, never see duplicate cards, and keep phone-watch dismissal sync once the watch posts its own notifications? Name the exact Jetpack / AndroidX classes and methods.

expected_behavior: Prescribes testing with the companion phone app force-stopped/killed (adb shell am force-stop <pkg>) while the phone screen is locked/off.

Identifies both (1) WindowManager$BadTokenException ('Unable to add window -- token null is not valid; is your activity running?') if a background-bound WearableListenerService attempts Dialog.show() / bottom-sheet attachment without a running Activity, and (2) silent Android 10+/14+ Background Activity Launch (BAL) blocking if it calls startActivity() directly instead of posting a notification (e.g., with setFullScreenIntent).
cases.prompt:
A Wear OS watch app implements first-run sign-in via the Wear Data Layer (`MessageClient`) to its companion Android phone app, where the user is already signed in:
1. User opens the watch app and taps 'Sign in on phone'; the watch shows 'Check your phone' with a 3-emoji verification sequence.
2. On the paired Android phone, the companion app displays a confirmation sheet with the matching 3 emojis and 'Approve' / 'Deny' buttons.
3. Tapping 'Approve' sends the auth session back to the watch.

QA tests with both apps open on screen and sign-in succeeds every time. Before tapping 'Sign in on phone' on the watch, what phone process and screen state should QA force via `adb` to uncover first-run failures masked by having the phone app open, and what specific phone-side crashes or silent OS blocks is that test catching?
